content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Understanding Injection Attacks: SQLi, Command Injection, and XSS"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Injection vulnerabilities remain among the most critical security risks in modern web applications. They occur when untrusted data is sent to an interpreter as part of a command or query. In this tutorial, we will explore three major types of injection attacks from an ethical hacking perspective: SQL Injection (SQLi), Operating System Command Injection, and Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. SQL Injection (SQLi)"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"SQL Injection occurs when user input is directly concatenated into a database query string rather than being handled via parameterized statements. This allows an attacker to manipulate the query structure, bypass authentication, or exfiltrate sensitive data."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = 'admin' AND password = 'password';"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"If an application constructs the query insecurely, an input like ' OR '1'='1 can alter the logic to return true for all records."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '' OR '1'='1' AND password = '';"},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Operating System Command Injection"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Command injection happens when a web application passes unsafe user-supplied data to a system shell. If input validation is missing, attackers can chain arbitrary commands using operators like semicolons, ampersands, or pipes."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"ping -c 4 127.0.0.1; cat /etc/passwd"},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) occurs when an application includes untrusted data in a web page without proper validation or escaping, allowing attackers to execute malicious scripts in the victim's browser context."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Stored XSS: The malicious script is permanently stored on the target server, such as in a database or comment section."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Reflected XSS: The malicious script is reflected off a web server, typically via a URL parameter or error message."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"DOM-based XSS: The vulnerability exists in client-side code rather than server-side code."},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"<script>alert('XSS Vulnerability Detected');</script>"},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Mitigation and Prevention Strategies"},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use Prepared Statements (Parameterized Queries) to prevent SQLi."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Avoid invoking OS commands directly. Use safer API alternatives or strict allow-lists for command execution."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Context-aware output encoding and input sanitization to neutralize XSS payloads."}]
